content.value:
A flywheel is a spinning mass used to launch game pieces. The goal: spin a GoBILDA motor at 4000 RPM and hold it.

Open FlywheelConfig.java. All tuning constants are defined here: motor type, target RPM, and PID/feedforward coefficients — all set to zero.

Flywheel.java builds a PIDController and a SimpleMotorFeedforward from those constants, then combines them in periodic().

FlywheelTuningOpMode.java displays the target vs actual RPM in telemetry.

Use the Programming Board robot config for a single motor named "motor".

Instead of using MotorEx's built-in velocity control (setVeloCoefficients / setFeedforwardCoefficients), you build the controller by hand with SolversLib's PIDController and SimpleMotorFeedforward classes.

Open Flywheel.java and read periodic():

1. Measure — read the current velocity in ticks/sec.

2. Feedforward — feedforward.calculate(targetVelocity) predicts the voltage needed for the target speed (kS + kV × velocity).

3. PID — pid.calculate(currentVelocity, targetVelocity) corrects the error (target − current).

4. Combine — add the PID and feedforward outputs. Both are already in volts, so the sum is your desired voltage. There is no max-ticks conversion.

5. Compensate — motor.set(desiredVoltage / voltage): divide your desired voltage by the actual voltage, the same formula from the voltage compensation lesson.

Why build it yourself? Two reasons:

More control — you can see and change every step: clamp the output, log intermediate values, or swap in a different controller. The built-in controller hides all of that.

Correct voltage compensation — the built-in velocity control calls setPower((pid + ff) / maxTicks) with no battery compensation. When the battery sags, your tuned constants become wrong. Building it yourself lets you divide the desired voltage by the actual battery voltage, so the flywheel holds speed at any battery level.

steps.title: Step 1: Find kS — overcome static friction

content.value:
kS is the minimum voltage needed to just barely start the motor spinning, in volts.

The feedforward output is added directly to the PID output as volts. A kS of 0.1 means the feedforward contributes 0.1V at rest — enough to break static friction.

In FlywheelConfig, keep kV, kP, kI, kD at 0.

Increase kS from 0. Start at 0.1. Increase in steps of 0.05. Rebuild each time.

Watch the RPM telemetry. Stop when the flywheel just barely starts to spin — RPM should be very low, 50-200.

Too high: the flywheel spins faster than needed from static friction alone.

Too low: the motor doesn't move at all.

steps.title: Step 2: Find kV — map velocity to power

content.value:
kV converts target velocity into feedforward voltage. In periodic(), feedforward.calculate(targetVelocity) returns kS + kV × targetVelocity, all in volts.

Keep your kS value. Keep PID at 0.

At 4000 RPM the flywheel spins at ~1867 ticks/sec (4000 RPM × 28 CPR ÷ 60). The voltage needed to hold a speed is roughly proportional to that speed, so kV ≈ 14V / maxTicksPerSec = 14/2800 = 0.005.

Start kV at 0.002. Increase in steps of 0.001.

With kV=0.005: ff = kS + 0.005 × 1867 = kS + 9.3V — enough voltage for ~4000 RPM.

If RPM is too low, increase kV. If it overshoots, decrease kV.

Goal: feedforward alone (kS + kV, no PID) gets within ~500 RPM of target.

steps.title: Step 3: Tune kP — close the gap with PID

content.value:
Now add kP. Feedforward got you close; PID fine-tunes.

Start with kP = 0.005. Increase until RPM oscillates around the target, then back off.

The oscillation should stay within ~50 RPM of the target.

Good: RPM holds steady at target with minor correction.

Too high kP: wild swings, audible "hunting". Too low: drifts slowly.

Optionally add a small kD to dampen bounce and kI to eliminate steady offset. But kS + kV + kP alone should get you very close.

The tuning order matters:

kS first: without breaking friction, nothing else works.

kV second: feedforward handles most of the work, so PID's job is small.

kP last: PID fills the remaining gap.

Your FlywheelConfig now holds the correct constants. In a real robot, you'd tune once, save these values, and never touch them again.

Because you built the controller yourself, periodic() runs the whole loop every cycle:

pidOutput + feedforwardOutput → desiredVoltage → desiredVoltage / voltage → motor.set(...)

Feedforward handles known physics, PID handles what the model misses, and voltage compensation handles battery drain. The built-in controller gives you the physics, but only a hand-built one gives you the control to apply voltage compensation correctly.
